meta.blurb: Broke and trying to write a play, Mr Bedford meets his neighbour Cavor, who has made a metal that blocks gravity. Soon they are flying to the Moon, where insect-like beings live below ground and their ruler wants to know about Earth.
meta.bible: Mr Bedford: the narrator, a practical businessman who has lost his money, who goes to Lympne to write a play; clever, greedy and brave. Cavor: a small, bald, brilliant and absent-minded scientist, who invents cavorite; kind, curious and too honest. Gibbs: Cavor's servant, who grows suspicious. Julius Wendigee: a Dutch scientist who receives Cavor's wireless messages. Selenites: the insect-like people of the Moon, each shaped from childhood for one task. Grand Lunar: the wise ruler of the Selenites, with a small body and a huge head. Mooncalves: huge soft animals that the Selenites herd and eat. Cavorite: a substance that blocks gravity; the story's invention. Lympne: a village in Kent. Kent: the county. Littlestone: the Kent beach where Bedford lands. Holland: where Wendigee lives. England. Earth. Moon. Greek. Rules of the story: the sphere has shutters of cavorite; with all shutters closed it is free of every pull, and an open shutter lets the nearest great body pull it; in this story air freezes on the Moon at night and melts at dawn. Voice and tone: a lively, wry adventure told by Bedford, funny at first, then wondering, then dark; suspense and wonder, no gore.

B1B2: Mr Bedford has lost all his money in business, and he has gone to the quiet village of Lympne in Kent. He hopes to write a play, which he thinks might earn him a fortune.
Bedford's neighbour is a small, bald man named Cavor, who is always in a hurry. He talks fast and forgets everything except his work, and Bedford soon learns that he is a scientist.
Cavor invites Bedford into his untidy laboratory, which is full of glass tubes and strange machines. He seems both proud and nervous, like a child who has a wonderful secret.
Cavor explains that light and heat can be stopped by screens, and he believes that gravity can be stopped, too. After years of work, he has made a metal that the Earth cannot pull down.
Bedford, who always thinks of profit, sees that cavorite could be worth a fortune. He asks to be Cavor's partner, and the scientist, who needs money for his work, agrees.
In the hot shed, the two men prepare a large sheet of cavorite and leave it to cool in a furnace. Cavor warns Bedford that something very odd may happen when it is ready.
Suddenly the sheet lifts off the floor as if it weighed nothing, and it rushes upward. It breaks through the roof of the shed, and a great wind blows through the room.
Cavor realises that a ship lined with cavorite could travel through space. He says calmly that he wants to go to the Moon, and Bedford, who has never heard such a thing, can only stare.
Cavor draws a plan for a metal sphere with thick glass windows and cavorite shutters. With every shutter closed, nothing will pull on the ship, and with one open, a planet will draw it that way.
Bedford and Cavor hire workmen to build the sphere in an empty house on the marsh, and they pay them well to keep quiet. Cavor's servant, Gibbs, grumbles about the noise and the mess.
The two men fill the sphere with tins of food, cans of water and cylinders of air. They also pack warm clothes, a few tools and some books, for the journey will be cold and long.
Gibbs, Cavor's servant, begins to ask questions and to look at the sphere with suspicion. The partners decide not to wait any longer, and they choose the very next night for their departure.
At night, Cavor and Bedford climb through the round door and bolt it behind them. Cavor opens a shutter, and the sphere shoots upward and away from the Earth.
Inside the sphere, nothing has any weight, and the two men float gently in the air. Bedford laughs and then feels sick, but Cavor is as happy as a child.
Through a window they see the Earth growing smaller, until it looks like a great bright disc in the dark. Bedford feels a pang of fear and a strange pride that he has come so far.
Days pass in the silence of space, and the stars shine harder than they ever do on Earth. When the sun is blocked out, the cold is bitter, and the two men wrap themselves in blankets.
Cavor opens and closes the shutters one by one, and the sphere changes its course. Slowly the Moon, a great pale ball scarred with craters, grows larger in the window.
As the Moon draws close, Cavor opens the shutters again so that the sphere can fall gently toward the surface. Below them lies a dark and silent land of rocks and shadows.
With a gentle bump, the sphere lands in a great crater, and the long journey is over. Outside, it is night, and the cold is far worse than anything on Earth.
As the sun rises over the edge of the crater, the heat begins to melt a thin white coat of frozen air. A cloud of mist rises from the ground, and the whole landscape begins to change.
As the warmth increases, brown seeds crack open and little green shoots push out of the ground. Within a few hours, the plants have grown tall enough to cover the whole floor of the crater.
Wearing warm clothes, Cavor and Bedford open the door and step out onto the Moon. Because everything weighs much less there, they can leap many yards in a single bound.
Cavor and Bedford walk among plants of many shapes, some like cactus and some like huge mushrooms. Cavor, as always, wants to look at everything, but Bedford is hungry.
Bedford is so hungry that he eats a piece of the strange fungus, although Cavor warns him not to. It makes him feel wild and happy, and he laughs and shouts for a long time.

In the distance, a herd of large, soft animals, which Cavor calls Mooncalves, moves across the plain. Behind them walks a thin creature with a long stick, and the two men realise that they are not alone.
Before the visitors can decide what to do, many Selenites rush up and surround them. The men fight, but they are overwhelmed, and the Selenites lead them to a hole in the ground.
The Selenites lead their prisoners down a long, dark tunnel into the Moon. The air grows warm and damp, and a faint blue light shines from somewhere far below.
Inside the Moon is a giant cavern full of light, machinery and thousands of busy Selenites. The visitors have never seen a place so strange, and they cannot take their eyes off it.
Cavor soon notices that each Selenite has a different shape and a different job. Some have huge hands for work, and others have enormous heads and thin bodies for thinking.
The Selenites keep their Mooncalves in great sheds, and they eat them as people on Earth eat cows. Their machines are clean, silent and clever, and they do much of the work.
Cavor draws circles, triangles and numbers on the floor, hoping to show that the visitors can think. A Selenite studies the drawings and answers with some signs of its own.
Cavor begins to learn a few words of the Selenite language, and he is delighted. Bedford, however, is uneasy and keeps saying that they must find the sphere and escape.
Bedford warns Cavor that the Selenites may see them as dangerous strangers, and he says they must act now. At last the scientist agrees, though he is sad to leave so many wonders behind.
The escape begins well, but soon a crowd of Selenites sees the two men and chases them. In the fighting and the darkness, Bedford and Cavor lose each other.
Alone in the tunnels, Bedford hides in a dark corner while the Selenites hunt for him. He feels more lonely than he has ever felt, and he fears that Cavor has been caught.
After many hours Bedford finds a long passage that slopes upward, and he sees a faint gleam of sunlight at the top. He climbs toward the light as fast as he can, with his heart pounding in his chest.
Bedford stands on the surface of the Moon, shivering in the thin, cold air. He is hungry, weak and alone, and he cannot see any sign of the sphere.
After a long search, Bedford finds the sphere half hidden by plants, and he climbs inside. He knows that he must leave Cavor behind, and he feels deeply ashamed.
Bedford opens and closes the shutters as he has seen Cavor do, and the sphere leaves the Moon. After many days alone, the Earth grows larger in the window, and he nearly weeps with joy.
The sphere drops from the sky and splashes into the sea close to a beach in Kent. Bedford, half drowned and shaking, struggles to the shore, and the empty sphere rises into the sky and is gone.
Bedford tells the people on the beach what has happened, but they only laugh or look at him with pity. He has no proof, because the sphere is gone and Cavor is far away.
Far away in Holland, a scientist named Julius Wendigee hears strange signals on his wireless set. They seem to come from space, and when he decodes them, he finds that they are in English.
In his first messages, Cavor says that he is alive and well on the Moon. He has escaped from the Selenites for the moment, and he is writing quickly because he does not know how long he has.
Cavor describes the Selenite world as ordered and clever, with each person made for one task. At its head is the Grand Lunar, a wise ruler with a small body and an enormous head.
The Grand Lunar, curious about the visitor, asks Cavor many questions about the Earth. Cavor, who likes to answer questions honestly, explains how people live there.
When the Grand Lunar asks about war, Cavor tells him the truth about the armies, the guns and the many quarrels of Earth. The ruler is troubled, and he asks again and again who has the power.
Cavor begins to see that his honesty may have put the Earth in danger. In his last messages he writes in a hurry, and he says that he no longer knows whether he is a guest or a prisoner.
One night a message begins as usual, and then it stops in the middle of a sentence. Wendigee waits all night beside his set, but nothing more arrives.
Bedford and Wendigee wait for weeks and then months, looking at the Moon and hoping for a new message. None ever comes, and they begin to fear that Cavor has been silenced.
Bedford finishes writing his story, although he cannot say what has become of Cavor. He looks at the quiet Moon and wonders whether anyone looks back at him.
C1C2: Mr Bedford, a businessman whose schemes had all collapsed, retired to the quiet village of Lympne in Kent with hardly a penny to his name. He had decided to write a play, a thing he knew nothing about, in the hope that it would restore his fortunes without costing him anything. The marsh stretched peacefully below his window, and for a short time he believed that his troubles were over.

Bedford's nearest neighbour was a small, restless man named Cavor, who wore a battered hat and walked as if the world were moving too slowly for him. He was brilliant, absent-minded and entirely unaware of how strange he seemed, and when he spoke, he did so in a rapid, breathless stream. Bedford, who was bored and curious, soon came to know that this odd fellow was a serious man of science.

Before long, Cavor invited Bedford into his untidy laboratory, a shed crowded with glass, wires, furnaces and half-finished experiments. He moved among his instruments like a child with a wonderful secret, anxious to share it yet afraid of being laughed at. Bedford, who had expected nothing at all, found himself drawn in by the little man's enthusiasm.

Cavor explained that light, heat and even electricity can be stopped by a suitable screen, and that he had long believed gravity could be stopped in the same way. After years of patient work, he had made a new alloy that cut off the pull of the Earth, and the substance was soon known as cavorite. Bedford, who knew little of science, understood only that something remarkable had been achieved.

Bedford, whose thoughts were never far from money, saw at once that a metal which cancelled weight might be worth a fortune. He proposed that the two of them become partners, with himself providing the business sense and Cavor the science. The little scientist, who needed funds for his experiments and cared nothing for profit, agreed without any hesitation.

In the hot, noisy shed, the two men prepared a large sheet of cavorite and set it to cool in the heat of a furnace. Cavor, who had made the test many times in smaller form, warned his partner that something very odd might happen when the sheet was ready. Bedford, sweating and half deafened by the roar of the fire, waited with a strange mixture of excitement and doubt.

Suddenly the sheet lifted from its stand as lightly as a feather, and before either man could move, it rushed upward and broke through the roof of the shed. A great wind swept through the room, whirling papers and dust and tools into the air, and the two men were thrown into confusion. When they recovered, the sheet was gone, and nothing was left of the roof but a large and ragged hole.

Cavor, standing under the broken roof, had a sudden and wonderful idea, for if a sheet of cavorite could rise, then a room lined with it could travel into space. He announced, with the calmness of a man ordering lunch, that he intended to visit the Moon and that Bedford was welcome to come. Bedford, who had never in his life heard a stranger proposal, thought for a moment and then agreed.

Cavor sketched a plan for a round ship of steel and thick glass, with windows covered by shutters of cavorite that could be opened and closed at will. With every shutter closed, he explained, the sphere would be free of every pull, and when one was opened, the nearest great body would draw it that way. In this manner, he said, they would be able to steer a course through the heavens as a sailor steers across the sea.

The sphere was built in an empty house on the edge of the marsh, by workmen who were paid well and told to ask no questions. Day after day, the sound of hammers rang out across the fields, and Cavor's servant, Gibbs, grumbled at the noise and the mess that had invaded his master's quiet life. Bedford, who had never done so much work in his life, felt both proud and anxious as the great steel ball took shape.

The partners loaded the sphere with tins of food, cans of water and heavy cylinders of compressed air, together with warm clothes and a few simple tools. Cavor had calculated every pound of weight to the ounce, and Bedford was amazed at the little man's skill in fitting a whole journey into so small a space. The preparations were nearly finished at last, and the date of their departure was coming uncomfortably near.

Gibbs, the servant, had become uncomfortably curious, and the partners feared that he might talk to the neighbours or even to the newspapers. Rather than risk the loss of their secret, they agreed to leave at the earliest moment, and they chose the very next night. Bedford spent the day in a state of nervous excitement, saying goodbye in his mind to everything he knew.

Under the cover of darkness, Cavor and Bedford climbed through the narrow door of the sphere and bolted it behind them, shutting out the Earth. Cavor, after a final look at his instruments, opened a shutter, and at once the great ball rose into the air and left the ground behind. Bedford, clinging to a railing, had the sudden feeling that his stomach had been left on the marsh.

Within the sphere, nothing seemed to have any weight, and the two men drifted about the chamber like fish in a tank. Bedford, after a first fit of laughter, began to feel dizzy and unwell, while Cavor floated peacefully, absorbed in his notes and instruments. It was a strange, silent, dreamlike state, and neither man could quite believe that it was real.

Through the windows they could see the Earth growing smaller, until it hung in the darkness like a great shining disc, wrapped in cloud and crossed by oceans. Bedford was seized by a sudden pang of fear, for everything he had ever known was now behind him, and by a strange pride that he had come so far. Cavor, however, stared in silence at the wonderful sight below them, and his face was shining with delight.

As the days passed, the sky around them became an enormous blackness, and the stars shone with a hard, steady brilliance that no one on Earth had ever seen. When the sunlight was shut out by the shutters, the cold crept in through the steel walls, and the two men huddled together beneath their blankets. Bedford began to see that a journey of this kind needed more courage than he had known he possessed.

With great care, Cavor opened and closed the shutters one at a time, and the sphere, answering to the invisible pulls on every side, slowly turned toward its goal. The Moon, once a small white lamp in the sky, grew into a vast pale world scarred by mountains and craters and seamed with long dark shadows. Bedford watched it with his heart in his mouth, for he now began to wonder whether they would ever be able to land.

As the Moon drew near, Cavor adjusted the shutters so that the sphere would sink slowly toward its surface instead of falling like a stone. Below them lay a dark, silent land of jagged rocks and shadowed hollows, lit only by the pale glimmer of the stars. The two men, tired and anxious, held their breath as the ground came up to meet them.

With a soft, almost tender bump, the sphere came to rest on the floor of a great crater, and the long voyage was over. Outside, it was the lunar night, and the cold that pressed against the steel walls was far more dreadful than any winter that Bedford had known. They had arrived, but they had arrived in the dark, in silence and in the middle of a world made of ice and stone.

When the sun finally rose above the rim of the crater, its heat began to melt a thin white coat of frozen air that had covered the ground during the night. Clouds of mist curled up from the ground, and the barren plain softened and glistened like a morning meadow after rain. Bedford and Cavor pressed their faces to the glass, hardly able to believe what they saw.

As the warmth increased, strange brown seeds, which had lain hidden for the whole of the night, cracked open and sent green shoots upward with astonishing speed. Within a few hours, they had grown into thick, fleshy plants that covered the crater floor like a new forest. Cavor, who was a scientist first of all, almost danced with delight at this extraordinary proof that the Moon was alive.

Wrapped in warm clothes, Cavor and Bedford opened the door of the sphere and stepped out onto the surface of the Moon, where the air, though thin, was just good enough to breathe. Because everything weighed so much less than on Earth, they were able to leap many yards at a time, laughing like schoolboys on a holiday. For a little while, in the joy of that strange new freedom, the two friends forgot their danger entirely.

They wandered among a bewildering garden of plants, some spiny like cactus, some round like enormous puffballs, and some like great swollen mushrooms that heaved in the heat. Cavor wished to stop and study every one, scribbling notes at a furious pace, while Bedford, whose stomach had begun to growl, grew restless and ill-tempered. They had not eaten since leaving Earth, and the smell of the strange fungi was unexpectedly tempting.

Bedford, unable to resist any longer, broke off a piece of the soft fungus and swallowed it, although Cavor begged him to wait. For a moment nothing happened, but then a wild, reckless gaiety swept over him, and he began to shout and sing and boast of the great deeds he would perform on the Moon. By the time the effect had worn off, he was thoroughly ashamed of himself, and he promised never to do such a foolish thing again.

In the distance, a herd of huge, soft animals, which Cavor named Mooncalves, was moving slowly across the plain, driven by a creature that walked on two long, thin legs. It was not a beast, for it carried a long stick and moved with purpose, and its body glittered like the shell of a great insect. Cavor and Bedford crouched behind a rock, understanding at last that the Moon had inhabitants, and that they were not human.

Before the two men could decide what to do, a crowd of the creatures, whom Cavor named Selenites after the Greek word for the Moon, rushed out and surrounded them. The visitors struggled and shouted, but the Selenites were strong and many, and they were swiftly overpowered. When they looked round for the sphere, it had disappeared, and there was no way back to the Earth.

Without a word, the Selenites led their captives down a long, winding tunnel into the heart of the Moon, where the air grew warm and damp and the darkness was broken only by a faint glow. Bedford's legs trembled, and even Cavor, who was usually unafraid, kept close to his friend and said little. At the bottom of the passage they came out into a great hall, and what they saw there took their breath away.

Inside the Moon lay an enormous cavern, glowing with a cold light and thronged with thousands of busy Selenites, who crowded the bridges and stairways and the great machines. It was a world that had been shaped by minds as clever as human ones, and perhaps cleverer, and it was full of marvels that neither visitor could understand. Cavor stared at it with the delight of a child, while Bedford stared with the wariness of a man who has seen how quickly a crowd can turn.

Cavor soon noticed that each Selenite had a different body, for the creatures were shaped from childhood to fit one task and one task only. The labourers had huge hands and tiny heads, while the thinkers, of whom there were many, had enormous brains and thin, feeble bodies. It seemed to Cavor an extraordinary system, efficient and orderly, but also a terrible thing, for it left no room for freedom or for any choice of one's own.

The Selenites kept their Mooncalves in vast sheds, feeding them and breeding them as farmers on Earth breed cattle, and the men soon learned that these animals were the main food of the underground world. Machines of astonishing delicacy carried out most of the heavy labour, humming and clanking quietly in the glowing halls. Bedford thought of the factories of England and realised that in many ways the Moon was far ahead.

Cavor, whose great hope was to speak with the beings of another world, knelt on the floor and drew circles, triangles and numbers in the dust. A tall Selenite studied the figures with interest, and after a time it replied with a few signs of its own, which showed that it understood mathematics at least as well as he did. For the first time, the two sides understood that their minds, at least, were alike.

As the days passed, Cavor began to learn the first words of the Selenite language, and every new word filled him with joy. Bedford, who was more practical and more frightened, kept insisting that they should find the sphere and escape before their hosts changed their minds. The quarrel between the two men grew sharper, for one of them longed to stay and the other to go home.

Bedford pointed out that the Selenites, who were so orderly and so cold, might one day decide that two strange visitors were too dangerous to keep, and he begged Cavor to act while there was still time. The scientist, torn between curiosity and good sense, agreed with great reluctance to attempt an escape. Together they chose a moment when the guards were looking away and slipped quietly toward a dark passage.

The escape began well, but within a few minutes an alarm sounded, and a crowd of Selenites came pouring out of every doorway in pursuit. Bedford and Cavor fought and ran side by side through the glowing caves, but in the darkness and confusion, they were separated and could not find each other again. Bedford, hearing a distant cry that might have been his friend's, dared not turn back.

Alone in the maze of tunnels, Bedford crept into a dark recess and lay still while the sound of hunting feet passed him by. He had never felt so lonely in his whole life, and he was haunted by the thought that Cavor had been captured, or worse. When the noises faded, he knew that he must find a way to the surface, whatever the cost.

After many hours of wandering, Bedford found a long passage that sloped steadily upward, and at the far end of it he saw a faint gleam of sunlight. He climbed toward it as fast as his tired legs would carry him, with the whole Moon seeming to hold its breath. When he stepped out into the open, he was blinded for a moment by the brilliant glare.

Bedford stood on the surface of the Moon, shivering in the thin, cold air, with the vast plain stretching away on every side. He was exhausted and hungry, and he saw no trace of Cavor, no sign of the Selenites, and no hint of the sphere that was his only hope. Yet he remembered the shape of the crater where they had landed, and he began, slowly, to search.

After a long and anxious search, Bedford discovered the sphere half hidden among the strange plants, and he climbed inside with a cry of relief. He knew that without Cavor he could not be certain of finding his way, and he was ashamed to leave his friend behind. But he also knew that if he stayed, he would die, and so he steadied his nerves and made ready for the journey home.

Remembering all that he had watched Cavor do, Bedford opened and closed the shutters until the sphere rose from the Moon and turned its face toward home. The days that followed were the loneliest of his life, but at last the Earth swelled in the window, blue and green and bright, and the sight brought tears to his eyes. He was returning to a world that had no idea what he had seen, and to a life that could never be the same.

In the early morning, the sphere plunged out of the sky and fell into the sea not far from the beach at Littlestone in Kent, throwing up a great column of water. Bedford, half drowned and shaking with cold, struggled out through the door, and the sphere, lightened of his weight, rose into the sky and was lost for ever. Fishermen who happened to be on the beach waded into the surf to help him, and he sat on the shingle, laughing and crying together.

Bedford told the fishermen everything, from the first shutter to the last, but they either laughed at him or looked at one another with pity. He had no proof of any kind, for the sphere was gone, and Cavor, the only other witness, was about a quarter of a million miles away. He decided, wearily, that he would have to wait for some better opportunity to be believed.

In Holland, a scientist named Julius Wendigee, who had been experimenting with a wireless set, began to receive strange signals that seemed to come from beyond the Earth. When he decoded them, he found, to his amazement, that they were in English, and that they were signed with the name of Cavor. The signals were coming from a man who was still alive, and who had somehow built a wireless set on the Moon.

In the first of his messages, Cavor announced that he was alive and well, and that he had escaped the attentions of the Selenites long enough to set up his instruments. He wrote hurriedly and with great excitement, knowing that his time might be short, and he promised to describe everything that he had seen. The words, tapped out across a quarter of a million miles of space, seemed to Wendigee like the voice of a ghost.

Cavor's later messages described a society as orderly as a hive of bees, in which every citizen was shaped for one task and asked for nothing else. At its head stood the Grand Lunar, a ruler of immense wisdom whose body was small and weak but whose enormous head held a mind of great power. Cavor wrote of him with a mixture of awe and unease, as of someone who sees too much.

The Grand Lunar, curious about the strange visitor, questioned Cavor for hours, and Cavor, who could never refuse an honest question, explained to him how life was lived on Earth. He described cities, farms, ships and laws, and the ruler listened in silence, recording each answer with the help of his clever servants. Cavor seemed pleased to be a teacher, and he did not yet see where this conversation might lead.

When the Grand Lunar asked about war, Cavor told him honestly about armies, guns and the endless quarrels between the nations of Earth. The ruler grew thoughtful and troubled, and he asked again and again who held the power, who obeyed, and how a world so full of conflict could possibly be controlled. Cavor, in his innocence, did not understand that every answer was making the Moon's people more afraid of mankind.

At last Cavor began to understand that his frankness might have put the whole Earth in danger, for the Selenites, being cautious and clever, would never leave a rival world unwatched. His messages became shorter and more anxious, and he wrote that he was no longer sure whether he was a guest or a prisoner. Wendigee, reading the signals with a sinking heart, could do nothing but wait and hope that his distant friend would soon speak again.

One night, a new message began as usual, in Cavor's careful and hurried style, and then it stopped in the middle of a sentence. Wendigee sat all night beside his set, listening to the faint hiss of the empty sky, but nothing more came. The silence that followed was, for the Dutch scientist, the heaviest and the most mysterious that he had ever known.

Bedford travelled to Holland to meet the man whose set had carried the news, and the two of them sat up many nights, listening for the signal and looking at the Moon. Weeks passed, then months, and nothing came, and with every silent night their hope grew a little thinner. They began to fear that Cavor had been silenced, either by accident or by the will of the Selenites.

And so Bedford laid down his pen, with the story told but its most important question unanswered, for no one on Earth could say what had become of Cavor. On clear nights he still looked up at the pale face of the Moon, wondering whether his friend was alive, and whether any eye was watching the Earth from that silent distance. It was a story of wonder, and also of warning, about how easily knowledge can run ahead of wisdom.
